title: Quality of earnings and normalization
summary: Test whether the earnings are real and repeatable by examining each add-back and normalizing the numbers.
outcomes: Explain what a quality-of-earnings review tests.
Classify add-backs as supported, questionable or rejected.
Normalize owner pay, rent and one-time items.

lessons.title: What quality of earnings means
lessons.body:
The seller's cash flow figure is a claim. A quality-of-earnings (QoE) review asks two questions about it:

1. **Is it real?** Do the numbers tie to bank statements, tax returns and invoices?
2. **Will it repeat?** Will the business earn this under a new owner, at today's costs?

For larger deals, buyers and lenders often pay an accounting firm for a formal QoE report. For smaller deals, you may do a lighter version yourself and then confirm the key points with your accountant. Either way, the habits are the same.

## Proof of cash
Compare reported revenue with deposits in the bank statements for the same months. Large unexplained gaps deserve questions. This is one of the simplest and most useful tests you can run.

lessons.title: Add-backs and normalization
lessons.body:
Add-backs are expenses the seller says will not continue under a new owner. Each one raises the earnings figure, and so the price. Treat every add-back as a claim that needs support.

## Common add-backs
- **Owner salary and benefits** (for SDE)
- **Personal expenses** run through the business, such as a family vehicle
- **One-time costs**, such as a lawsuit or a rebrand
- **Non-cash items**, such as depreciation (keep in mind that equipment still needs replacing)

## Normalization adjusts in both directions
Normalization also **lowers** earnings when costs are below market:
- The owner's relative works for less than a market wage.
- Rent is below market because the owner also owns the building, and a new lease will cost more.
- Maintenance has been deferred and will need spending soon.

## Sort each item
For each add-back, record the amount, the evidence and your decision: **supported**, **questionable** or **rejected**. Base your price on supported items only, and treat questionable ones as negotiation points.

## Practical output
Build an **adjusted earnings sheet** with reported earnings, each adjustment with its evidence, and your adjusted figure. Ask your accountant to review it before you rely on it.

practicalOutput.title: Adjusted earnings sheet
practicalOutput.description: A table that turns reported earnings into earnings you can defend, item by item.
steps: Start from reported pre-tax earnings for each year.
List every add-back with its amount and evidence.
Mark each add-back supported, questionable or rejected.
Add downward adjustments for below-market costs.
Calculate adjusted earnings and note the open questions for your accountant.

quiz.question: Which two questions does a quality-of-earnings review ask?
options: Is it real, and will it repeat?
Is it legal, and is it taxed?
Is it growing, and is it famous?
Is it cheap, and is it close by?
quiz.explanation: QoE tests whether earnings are accurate and sustainable under a new owner.

quiz.question: The owner's daughter works full-time for half the market wage. What does normalization do?
options: Lowers earnings to reflect a market wage
quiz.explanation: Below-market costs will rise under a new owner, so normalization lowers earnings.

quiz.question: What is a 'proof of cash' test?
options: Comparing reported revenue with bank deposits
Asking the seller to confirm in writing
quiz.explanation: Tying revenue to bank deposits is a simple test of whether the numbers are real.

quiz.question: How should you treat a questionable add-back?
options: Use it as a negotiation point until it is supported
quiz.explanation: Price on supported items; keep questionable ones open until evidence arrives.
